cues.text: Let us begin with section two: machine learning and neural networks.
Machine learning is a way of building systems that learn patterns from data rather than following rules that a person wrote out line by line.
The first big distinction is how the system learns, and that depends on what kind of feedback it receives.
Start with supervised learning.
Here the model trains on labelled input-output examples.
Each example pairs an input with the correct answer, which we call the label.
The model studies many such pairs and learns a mapping from inputs to outputs.
Supervised learning comes in two main forms.
Classification predicts categories.
A good example is fraud or not fraud: the model looks at a transaction and assigns it to one of those two categories.
Regression, by contrast, predicts numerical values.
Think of delivery time, or sales demand.
The question is not which category, but how much, or how long.
The source gives several example methods: decision trees, logistic regression and linear regression, support vector machines, and nearest-neighbour methods.
Notice that logistic and linear regression appear together, but the first is typically used for classification and the second for numerical prediction, in keeping with the distinction we just made.
Next, unsupervised learning.
This discovers structure without target labels.
Nobody tells the model the right answer; it looks for patterns by itself.
The source names three uses.
Clustering groups similar items together.
Dimensionality reduction compresses representations, meaning it expresses the data in a smaller, more compact form.
And anomaly detection can identify unusual patterns, items that do not fit what is normal.
Then there is reinforcement learning.
This learns action policies through interaction and rewards.
A policy is simply a rule for choosing actions.
The system acts, receives rewards, and gradually learns which actions earn more reward.
But here is an important warning from the source: poorly designed rewards can encourage unwanted behaviour.
If you reward the wrong thing, the system will faithfully pursue the wrong thing.
Now to neural networks.
A neural network consists of connected computational units arranged in layers.
Each unit does a simple job.
It combines its weighted inputs and a bias, and then applies an activation.
The weights say how much each input matters; the bias shifts the result; the activation is a function that transforms the combined value before passing it on.
Training is the process of adjusting the weights to minimise a loss function.
The loss function measures how wrong the model's predictions are, so minimising it means becoming less wrong.
This is often done using backpropagation and gradient-based optimisation.
Backpropagation works out how much each weight contributed to the error, and gradient-based optimisation uses that information to nudge the weights in a helpful direction.
The layers have different roles.
Input layers receive features, the measurable characteristics of the data.
Hidden layers learn representations, which are internal ways of describing the data that help with the task.
Output layers produce predictions.
When a network uses multiple layers, we call it a deep network.
Different architectures suit different problems.
CNNs, or convolutional neural networks, are useful for spatial patterns such as images.
Recurrent networks and LSTMs, which stands for long short-term memory networks, model sequences.
Transformers use attention for relationships between tokens, and they are widely used in language and in other domains.
GANs, or generative adversarial networks, use generator and discriminator training: one part generates, the other judges.
Generative models can also use other architectures besides GANs.
So how do we choose?
The source is clear: choose according to task, data, cost, interpretability and validation, not hype.
That brings us to the heading: model lifecycle and evaluation.
A model is not a one-off product.
It moves through a lifecycle, and the source lists the steps in order.
First, define the objective and acceptable errors, so you know what success means and how much error you can tolerate.
Second, collect lawful representative data, which means data obtained legally and that genuinely reflects the situation the model will face.
Third, clean and prepare features.
Fourth, split the data into train, validation and test datasets.
Fifth, train the model.
Sixth, validate it.
Seventh, deploy with human oversight where needed.
Eighth, monitor drift, latency and quality.
Drift is when the real world changes so the model's inputs or relationships no longer match what it learned; latency is how long it takes to respond.
Finally, retrain or retire the model when justified.
Two pitfalls deserve attention.
Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time enters training or evaluation, making results misleading.
The model appears brilliant in testing, but it was effectively given clues it will not have in real use.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-specific noise and generalises poorly.
It memorises quirks of the training data instead of learning patterns that carry over to new cases.
Now a worked example.
A fraud model flags 100 transactions, and 80 of them are actually fraudulent.
Separately, of 100 actual frauds, 80 are detected.
Let us name the counts.
True positives equal 80: these are frauds correctly flagged.
False positives equal 20: the model flagged 100, 80 were fraud, so 20 were legitimate transactions wrongly flagged.
False negatives equal 20: there were 100 actual frauds, 80 were caught, so 20 were missed.
Precision equals true positives divided by the sum of true positives and false positives.
That is 80 divided by 80 plus 20, which is 80 over 100, or 80 percent.
Precision answers: of everything flagged, how much was truly fraud?
Recall equals true positives divided by the sum of true positives and false negatives.
That is 80 divided by 80 plus 20, again 80 percent.
Recall answers: of all the real frauds, how many did we catch?
Accuracy also depends on true negatives, the legitimate transactions correctly left alone.
In highly imbalanced fraud detection, where fraud is rare, accuracy alone may hide poor detection.
A model could be right almost every time simply by calling nearly everything legitimate, while catching little fraud.
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
Here both are 80 percent, so F1 is 80 percent.
Finally, a risk threshold trades false positives against false negatives.
Setting it to flag more transactions catches more fraud but wrongly flags more legitimate ones.
Blocking every suspicious payment may protect funds but frustrate legitimate customers.
So monitor segment-level errors, meaning how the model performs for different groups of customers, and provide review and escalation paths.
And remember one last principle: correlation does not establish causation.
A pattern linking two things does not prove that one causes the other.
